title: QueryClick | Agencies.co Onboarding and Andy Day

sentences.text: Hi, Chris, how you doing?
Thank you, yes.
How are you?
Yeah, good, thank you.
Are you up in Scotland?
Edinburgh?
I'm indeed, yes.
Hey, Brian.
Hello.
There's Brian and Richard.
On his way.
There we go.
Nice to have you all on.
It's a pleasure to be here, Andy.
Yes, for us too.
Just to give you a quick overview on today's call.

We're using the content of the call to put together all of our marketing materials, obviously for myself and Ahmed and the rest of the team as well, to understand what the business does, what the unique, you know, processes are.
And the opportunity is that we're, we're selling to the potential buyers.
So we have a questionnaire but obviously, you know, we can, we can veer off course if you feel that there's some other stuff that we're, we're missing or is part of the story.
But basically we're looking for the whole sort of story arc, you know, how you got the business started and then what the services are, et cetera, et cetera.

We'll jump into that then after this call we'll make a number of requests for information for the data room, which doesn't have to be in depth right now because obviously this is the most pain in the ass stuff to do is actually building the data room.
But the majority of the financials and stuff that we need to understand what the value of the business is going to be so we can put the valuation together.
Any questions so far?
So straightforward.
It is, it is.
All right, brilliant.
Okay, so let's kick off.
So the first section really is just about the background of the business.
So could you tell us, Chris, how the business started and what the sort of founder story is?
Yeah, of course.
So I was working building freelance websites and was initially hired into a business called Big Mouth media in around 2005, 2006.
I was the first sort of technical person in there who could build websites.
There was 25 or so people there when I joined a couple of years later there was one and a half thousand, two thousand people.
We were the largest independent search marketing agency in the world for a time.
We're number one in search engines for the words SEO and search engine optimization.
During my time there, essentially I build out the technical SEO team, created a content department.
It wasn't a thing back then.
I used to hire people by literally advertising in local libraries because you couldn't really get copywriters for the web.
It wasn't, wasn't so much a thing back then.
I also created an inbound department again.
That's something that's much more commonplace now.
But this idea of developing high quality external links and so on.
So that was a very high growth period and I experienced it firsthand.
Built teams.
I had to integrate businesses that had been bought as well along the way.
But that business also was constrained by private equity funding.
The owner there was restricting headcount.
I felt we probably had the best quality product in the world at that point, but not necessarily the best service quality support.
So when it was acquired ultimately by Publicis it went through a few acquisitions and ended up in Publicis.
I exited around 2008, founded Query Click.
At that point, no external funding, just bootstrapped it with my own cash.
I felt that I probably had an inside track on the highest performance search optimization strategies that you could possibly build.

Having worked with the largest businesses in the world including Hilton Hotels, British Airways, Barclays Bank, Emirates Airlines, BBC paid enormous amounts of money for me to advise them on if they should migrate to BBC.com from co uk for the main BBC site.
So I simply decided with QueryClick to create some an agency that could deliver best quality service alongside best quality product.
That was our sort of foundation view in 2008 immediately started working with T Mobile and a number of financial institutions who recognized the quality of the offering.
Principally we were focused in on enterprise customers certainly initially, but also with a widening lens on retail.
So going outside of finance and telecoms picked up a lot of good quality brands along the way.
Built and delivered organic strategies for T Mobile as it migrated to incorporate orange and then become ee.
That was a migration.
We helped support with and delivered an uplift of 64 million pounds of organic revenue the year after it was completed as year on year increase in revenue.
Picked up BT as a customer, picked up Tesco as a customer.
And so that was about 10 years into our journey.
No external funding whatsoever.
Had built out, you know, a full service digital marketing agency, organic and paid media across the board.
Very high growth.
But also around about that point we had been looking at how we could use our R and D function to identify unique data opportunities.

So we have always sold ourselves by having know a best in class view of data, understanding the best way and ideally a unique way to identify the highest performance that you could possibly deliver from strategy.
So we sell ourselves on performance.
We have a flywheel we use internally to design our own internal growth strategies.
Our number one requirement is that we deliver customer success in their own language and we use that to make sure that we are actually getting things done with them.
Which moves the needle for performance and make sure that they expand their work with us and are happy.
Our R and D function had identified a number of different tools, some of which we still use to this day, so including Unified Search and Halo reporting tools which we see as unique to market.
Halo is something we still use today that is not discussed particularly in the industry.

It's a way of looking across paid and organic and understanding the click through rate behaviors and the influence of organic on paid and vice versa, as well as dynamic gap analysis on opportunities for growth, all sorted by revenue impact.
ROI impact for the customer helps drive integrated strategies.
We feel like we're probably best in class at that in the industry today.
But also we developed an interest in attribution.
So you'll be aware, of course we have a sister component to the business which is called Corviday.
It's an attribution platform.
It uses AI to rebuild digital marketing data that's separate part of the business from the services side.
But it developed out of the R and D function in there.

And the reason behind that was to allow us to solve a major problem for customers clearly, which was really understanding where their performance came from, where their revenue came from across organic and paid.
And so around nine years ago when I started looking at that issue with the R and D function, we identified that was an area that could take external investment.
And so we spent nine years in total delivering, developing and delivering what became the Corvadae technology and platform.
And about five years ago we took external investment to help realize that and feed that into that side of the business.
So for the last four or five years, I would say I've been working across both aspects of the business.

Services side has operated with plateaued revenues, not necessarily growing particularly, really running itself with some really strong individuals that are in leadership positions across the paid media and organic side of things.
Whilst I basically bootstrapped and built out a startup alongside it in Corvidate, which has now launched to market.
So a very high level.
That's the story of the business today.
Okay, yeah, thank you for that.
And so that kind of takes us up to the point where the businesses went in two different directions.
So just sort of remaining with Query Click then for now.
So how would you describe the Query Click business?
You said it was a full service digital marketing agency, but what is it today?
Yeah, it is still that today.
So we have a paid and organic delivery team and we also have a specialist who works across them making sure that we have unified strategy in play.
We operate as an extension of client teams.
We're fully remote first.
We have custom delivery of strategy for every client.
We work across a range of different sectors.
Retail is an important sector for us, but also finance business to business lead generation.
We have very strong expertise and customer base there as well.
And we essentially operate as a full service agency.
Okay, all right, we'll get into the clients in a second.
So now you are more focused on Corvide, is that correct?
That's where you're moving towards?
More focused on that?
Yes.
But still have a hand in both.
Okay, so your, your role Currently is in QueryClick.
Is.
Is what?
So currently I'm the CEO.
I sit across both aspects of the business on the services side to keep the focus in there.
I contribute towards leadership and strategy and I still have a hand in the technical organic priorities.
So going all the way back to that starting point, ensuring that we are putting together a technical strategy that is best in class for our customer base.
Okay, so who is the rest of the team now?
The director or key staff shareholders?
Yeah.
So we have Jackie Wakefield, who's the head of performance.

So she's the sort of most senior person that sits alongside me and ultimately is responsible for client delight and unified strategy for all of our customers and making sure that there's a fit to their.
Their business priorities and that we and the team are operating to those.
She has line management responsibility for the, the organic team, which I come to on the paid.
We have new paid media lead, actually, who's joining the business literally at the moment, Jenny spence.
She's got 15 years experience on the paid media side.
She's taking over the reins from a chap called Malcolm Gibb, who has been with the business for five, six years in that same role and himself has about 14 years of experience.
So Jenny owns basically paid media strategy, performance and again, fit to client priorities on the organic side.
And that team.
Jackie's got four reports ultimately in there, a couple of SEO managers, an exec and a technical who takes, you know, some strategy direction from myself.
And then on the paid side of things, Jenny has reports, four reports, principally Bethany, who is a paid senior paid media exec.
So just one step down from account manager.
We've got a paid account manager in Chris Alou.
We have a couple of consultants that run supporting in there that we associate against particular accounts.
And we also have a role that we're recruiting in there to backfill another employee at the moment.
So, okay, so.
So they're the main two people.
So if you were to get hit by a bus.
Chris?
Yeah.
What would happen to the business with Jackie and Jenny at the helm?
Do they, do they report to anywhere else or would they be the.
They report to me if I was hit by a bus.
I imagine Richard would get a phone call.
But ultimately they are responsible and run strategy and client connections.
So I'm in there really as a belt and braces contact for most customers and occasionally I get asked to give higher level advice for our customer base.
So for example, I sit in on wider QBR meetings sometimes and I get asked about more complex marketing challenges that are multi channel quite often.
So I've got quite a high profile in the industry.
People recognize the experience I've got.
So I get given the unusual questions like should I merge these brands?
I'm thinking of integrating with another business.
Could you help us assess the viability of things like that?
Plus also should we be, should we be spending more in media and some emerging channels, what's the market trend like, et cetera.
So ultimately the meat and drink of everything is delivered by Jackie and Jenny when she comes in.
But previously Malcolm and so those sort of queries that come in, the high level strategy conversations that you conduct, who do they come from?
So they're existing clients that basically sort of top out with the day to day stuff and then they come to you for the lead in the strategy conversations.
Yes.
Yeah, but only really occasionally and as I say, it's not day to day strategy that is entirely driven by those two other.
I also essentially am offering it as a, if you like, a value add, an aspect of, you know, the fact that we are 16 years old as business, we have really good visibility in the market.

We're seen as absolutely experts and specialists in, in the UK and so I'll sometimes get asked because of that to join in in some QBR discussions or offer you know, my, my crystal ball view on some strategic decisions that perhaps they need to take.
Got you.
So given that it sounds like you're, you're looking to focus on Corviday and move out the query click business.
Yeah.

Who would take over that role is, would Jackie then step up into a more, you know, sort of overseeing role across performance and running the business or, or is there a space for a CEO with similar experience to you to step in?
Jackie absolutely could.
I don't see any reason why she couldn't work just as effectively with another figurehead.
Both avenues are absolutely possible, I would argue.
Yeah.
So given the size of the business and a potential salary for that Figurehead.
Is it more plausible that Jackie would be the direction that a new owner?
I would have thought so, yeah.
And has that conversation been had with Jackie?
I mean how, how long she been in the business and how aware is she of this process?
She is aware of this process.
She's very comfortable with that and I think she would relish it.
She has been ahead of performance before in a previous role where she owned all of those responsibilities.
So she has no issue with that.
And as any, as any sort of training is the wrong word.
But is any sort of sharing of the oversight responsibilities that you have been discussed or you know, are you starting down that road with Jackie or is it just something that could easily happen?
Oh, it's something that could easily happen really.
I just fulfill the function of being another experienced head and there's no reason why she can't fulfill those functions today if she was asked to.

Just on that, Andy, if an acquirer comes in, I'm assuming they would have a senior member of staff who would potentially be that person they'd report into rather than having an independent business that runs by itself.
Acquirer comes in, they have management layer there that would then be able to work with them and perhaps a short earn out on Chris's side to make sure there's a smooth transition.
Is that feasible?
Yes, I mean it really does depend on the structure of the acquirer and what they're looking to do.
I mean it could be that we get an owner operator type that is using their own money to acquire a business and run it.
So in that case they probably want Chris out of the way as soon as possible.
But the sort of standard process would be if Chris was in that seat already, that they would want as long a handover process as possible, up to three to five years.
But obviously you guys would want a quick process so that Chris can sort of hand over, get an ear now and then step into the corviday role full time.

Yeah, I think given the size of our business though Andy, and the cost of Chris, that three to five years wouldn't be, I mean that wouldn't be a realistic position for somebody given the size of queer query clicks.
At least there's probably some level of handover.
I think realism would say that's nowhere near that sort of commitment.
Yeah, of course.
And we want to position the business that aligns with what your goals are.
So I mean, and it's absolutely fine for us to say, do you know what, Chris is pretty much out of the business.
He's looking to get out as quick, quickly as possible and maybe just put Chris into consultancy role for a short handover as possible.
But my thoughts are, you know, what is an acquirer going to ask about the current situation?

And my feeling is if we could start that process with the most likely his candidate to take on that role and step into it immediately, then we have a story ready to roll with a buyer and Chris can step out much quicker.
I think the quick handovers never tend to extend longer than sort of one year.
So sort of a middle point might be, you know, a 12 month handover.
But again, we would want to push for that as a, as a shared role because obviously Chris is involved in corvide as well.
So.

But I'm just thinking if she's the likely candidate, then maybe if we start that conversation early because what can happen I guess is when money comes onto the table is that then that's the moment when somebody feels they could be nervous or they might be able to use it at leverage, you know, for leverage at that point to get a better salary or whatever.
So the earlier we can have the conversation, it could be better, particularly if she knows that we're already talking.
So.
Okay, all right, so if we move on then, any, any offices outside of Edinburgh, what's the, where are all of the offices based, if any, or is it all remote?
It's pretty much all remote.
We use spaces.
So we have an office, an actual designated office in the Edinburgh spaces and then we have access to, to all of their offices across the uk.
So they've got one and a half thousand offices across the uk, so we just use appropriate ones.
So when we have meetings in London, quite often we use Liverpool Street.
There's a couple others that we like.
We make a feature of the fact that we're remote first and we can be where our clients are.
Okay, so that's a pretty easy contract to get out.
Although I would imagine there's no, excuse me, there's no office that's, you know, you've got a big long lease on or anything like that.
Okay, so what's the headcount in the business?
I think it sounds like there's some freelancers as well.
But what's the full time headcount and the freelance headcount?
I was just looking at that today, funnily enough, because we've got new people coming in and out as I've just mentioned.
So we've got nine on the services side.
And I think we can get all of this over to you as A pack so you can see everything and salary banding and so on.
Yeah, we'll need that for the data room for sure.
Yeah.
Okay, so there's nine.
Any others?
It's just nine full time for the services.
Yeah.
As I say, we've got some contractor work at the moment.
We've actually had a couple of new business wins so we've got a little bit of extra work that we're servicing at the moment, but yeah.
Okay, cool.
And in terms of business development, Chris, is that you who handles the clients as they come in?
Do you have a dedicated biz dev guy or.
Yeah, so we.
So we have in the growth team who mainly support the Corvador side of the business.
We have three.
So we have a paid media elite there, a chap called Pete.

He has got two business development reps who are kind of mid level I would say and they work through a pipeline that we have generated with marketing activity and marketing budget, principally event led and they, they manage the development of that pipeline.
They do provide services opportunities into, into the team and they then get pitched following our process and that pitch ultimately is led by Jackie.
I've been involved in one or two in the background again fulfilling the same role of background and outlining our philosophy and approach.
But ultimately all strategy comes from, from the team and on the paid media side has been Malcolm and will be Jenny when she's up and running middle of next month.
Okay.
So the inbound comes into your team that our actual corviday and they pass on basically through that pipeline.
Pipeline to the management and they pick it up then and write the, the pitch and.
And send it.
Yeah, yeah.
Okay.
Okay.
How would you sort of describe the culture of the business?
And I guess a secondary question would be how do you think that will change if you were to leave?
So we are very open I would say and I know everyone uses the word transparent but we really are.
We have a very supportive but also demanding culture.
In short, because we're remote.
First we measure people on performance outcomes.
So that means that we operate an OKR structure.

So objectives, key results reviewed quarterly, all of those are associated against business metrics for us and ultimately using our, I think I mentioned already the kind of flywheel and the philosophy that we have that customer success allows us to succeed that is translated into key results for every individual which are associated with their client performance.
And we review those using a 15, 5 structure.
So that is, you know, five minutes filling out just a kind of general feedback on what your plan was for the week.
And how you got on with it and 15 minutes discussing your line manager doing that every week and then having a more in depth, in depth review monthly.
Our those are kind of if you like our toolkit, we are very open.
We have a culture group which is self selected from the team.
They have a budget, they lead initiatives within the team on what they're going to do and how they celebrate success.

We have monthly awards which again get voted for by individuals and celebrated in mtams which we run monthly where we also kind of just share broadly strategy, you know, progress, client wins, success stories.
And I would say it's very, it's a as I say supportive but demanding.
If you aren't performing that quickly flushes out and there isn't a huge amount of space for people that don't perform in the business.
People that do.
We try and help develop them.
We run a nine day fortnight structure which is, you know, every two weeks at the discretion of your line manager.

You can get the second Friday off following a rota to make sure there's client support in place and that time is time you can use to work on personal development and usually that's a personal development plan every six months you're reviewing with your line manager as well.

So we have a lot of people really rate and value the fact that they are essentially treated as adults, allowed to manage to some extent their own, how they deliver their own time, their own ability, but also are held to quite high standard in terms of what they deliver and the way they engage with clients.
Um, I think it's a really great culture.
I mean I would unbiased but I've heard that from innumerable employees so I feel like I'd have to agree with it at this stage.
How big is the Corvid a team is that similar size?
So similar size, yeah.
And, and those sales guys sit on that side.
There's so six, six or so on the engineering side and then sales team and then finance, finance assistant and myself on that side.
Okay.
Who would you compare query click with?
Is there anybody else that you compete with?
Yeah, probably someone like crowd I would say we're nothing like as big as them.
We're a little bit more specialist.
We haven't invested in the growth of the business for the last five years.
So we essentially are, you know, we're winning where we are called out as part of our reputation rather than proactivity.
As I've mentioned with the, the way that the pipeline's focused in on Corvadae and it's really only generating out opportunities for services as an association.
So crowd would probably be a good, a good comparison.
And other modern agencies which have embraced, you know, using AI intelligently I guess would be the other way I could put it.
So we're open with our clients about, you know, how and why you can use AI technologies, particularly on the organic side, where the risks and dangers are, what the efficiencies are.
So we're quite agile in that respect and I think that probably puts us in line with some of the sort of second tier industry agency groups for comparison.
Okay, cool, thank you.
Okay, so just moving on into sort of the finance stuff.
We will send some requests, but just sort of ballpark numbers.
Well, it's probably better just to get all of that shared, I would have thought, in the pack.
I mean, Brian, Richard, I don't know what your thoughts are, but it is.
But we're just, we're just.
Yeah, we will request all that.
So really we just want to get into sort of what a client would look like, what, what kind of deal size, that sort of thing.
Yeah, okay.
Yeah, so we have a few different clients that are larger.
So call out, for example, Sally, Sally Beauty is a big client on the paid and organic side.
They actually have multiple brands in multiple regions.
So they're in 26 odd markets.
They would be spending something in the region of.
I feel like I should bring up the actual numbers rather than say them.
So I'll just say they're a larger customer.
Yeah, they operate B2B and D2C.
I don't know if you know their, their brand at all, but they have high street stores, but they also have hairdressers, hairdressing brands, multiple hairdressing brands.
So they have that aspect of their business also.
So they'll be spending, you know, tens of thousands with us per month.
They'll work to, you know, 12 month term retainers.
Similar story for another larger customer.
So first mortgage, they actually just extended for three years.
So they work across largely paid with us, but also bits of organic support, particularly on the technical side, gets brought in now and again, they're spending again.
So similar sort of tens of thousands a month with us to you, Chris.
So those, those two large clients, what, what was with the business generating revenue from those on a monthly basis?
Well, this is where.
You don't know.
Overall you're talking about 1.2 to 1.4 million per annum across the whole customer base.
They're a reasonably large portion of that.
All right, we'll get into it on the pack then if you got it.
Prepared that's probably better I think I just don't like giving a slightly off number and I don't have the current pack in front of me.
Yeah, it's just a feel for the numbers.
If you, if you haven't got them to, to mind then that's fine.
But it just is.
Sorry, I've been back to back today.
I would have otherwise.
Yeah.
Again just ballpark really is what we're looking for.
But that's, that's fine.
Don't worry about it.
We'll, we'll take it from the financials.
Okay.
You've mentioned a couple of big brands there.
Is there anybody else that kind of.
You enjoy working with or sort of you're known for you got selling?
Yes.
So Aggreko is probably a good example.
So we've actually been working with Aggreko for just coming into a decade now.
So Aggreko again multinational.
We principally work with our US team.
We recently just added the organic to their services on our side.
So they run paid media and organic and we've added in Canada as well into the mix.
So really nice.
Great customer, very you know, specific area.
You know it's something where you'll have some of their contracts are you know, eight figure contracts that they've won through digital activity.
You know they end up doing things like powering the Olympics, powering the Winter Olympics, powering some countries if you believe it, with diesel generators, have a really integrated team.

They used to have all countries with us and went through a procurement process where they were appointing an agency on the basis of having multinational support, that is offices globally to support the 36 countries they're in.
US demanded to stay with us.
So they, they have stayed with us and have recently indicated that the rest of the markets are now looking at tendering out again because of dissatisfactory the other agencies.
So you never know.
One day, potentially even before we have a transaction done, we might have brought those other markets back, back home.
So I think they're, they're a good example of a customer.
Another example, I think that's good affiliate.
So you know kitchen appliances, kitchen fittings, it's got that retail aspect to it.
But again specialist.
We're, we're just, we're very strong at making sure that we take on board customers who require performance is the simplest way I would describe it Andy.
That's what we sell ourselves on.
Quite early on in our pitching process we are establishing what we think growth would look like, how we would deliver it.
What the challenges on the client side are, what their requirements are, how their teams would need to operate to support it.
And we have that transparent approach deliberately as part of qualification in that sales process.
And so the customers we have sort of reflect that they, they typically are looking for growth.
If I can just add a little bit color there, Andy, Just a couple of other brand names from a getting people interested perspective.
We've got a retained contract with Vodafone.
Yeah.
And also with Sweaty Betty.
So obviously two brands that be aware of.
Our largest retained client is 250k per annum.
We've got a couple of, probably three at roughly 120k per annum and then a series of smaller ones.
Okay, so it's 1.2 and 250k is your largest one.
Because my next question was client concentration.
So that answers that.
So they make up 20%.
All right, so 20% for your large client and then the rest are 10% which is small enough.
All right.
Okay, so you mentioned before.
Just to clarify, those relationships then are handled by these two senior managers.
Once the client comes on board, they're the point of contact.
All right.
Not just those individuals, I should say, Andy, when we engage the whole team with our customers, so we don't hide people away.
Okay, Right.
Okay.
Let's get on to the reasons for why we're doing an M and A deal.
We've talked about the exit period that you're looking for in the handover.
So would that be six months?
Well, I mean, what is the ideal?
That we sell it and walk away on day one or what?
What are we looking for?
Six months at a stretch?
If there's some very strong reason for it, I would say.
Okay, all right, so.
So obviously we kind of half know this.
You developed a software solution, Corvette, and that's much more interesting to you personally.
You're looking to continue in that direction.
And the agency is what is just baggage from, from.
I mean, how would you describe it?
What.
Why is the agency no longer of interest to the group business?
The agency is very successful and I would say, I've probably said a few times, quote unquote, runs itself to Richard and Brian over the, over the years.
It's, it's very profitable, an excellent brand, an excellent business.
If someone wanted to, you know, establish real quality in the uk, it's a shortcut way to do that.
It's got, it's got real pedigree.
It is under exploited and ultimately, you know, having built Corvador to a point where it's now an incredibly high growth SaaS business.
I'm really obliged to make a decision about my stewardship across both sides.
So for me, yes, absolutely.
I'm invested in making sure that Corvidate grows and has the right attention and that QueryClick then is given a good pair of hands.
I think the team are really high quality.
Our customers are very, very loyal and are excellent customers too.
And so I want them to be in good hands also.
I think as well.

Just strategically, Andy, if you, if you're looking at why, why the business chosen now to do that, why an acquirer should feel comfortable with it, you know, the query click services business has helped grow the Carverday business.
There's no doubt.
Right.
Because it's been profitable.
So it's helped us grow that business out of where we are.
And at one and strategically they looked very complementary.

But I think what's become clear over the last 12 to 18 months as the carbody business has grown is that the customer base and the target base from a geographic through to scale of customer is different.
And so the overlap between those two customer bases is actually minimal.
And as a result the services business is suffering.

And so Chris has built as he identifies a really strong services business with a great brand and it will benefit from someone else taking that forward who can focus it and give it the time it needs to grow back.
Okay, all right, thanks for that, Richard.
Yeah, that's definitely useful.
And do you have like any ideas what types of business you'd like to sell into?
Does it matter?
I'm open minded, as I said.
I do want to see a good steward for the, for the team and for our customers.
I think that is important but I think that can come in many forms.
So I'm relatively open minded about what that might be.

There's the obvious candidates which I think you would probably be familiar with, Andy, where you think about large agency groups, you could think about bolt ons, you could think about, you know, UK presence for other strong independents that don't necessarily have that.
I think all of those are certainly very reasonable.
I've actually also had sort of interesting conversation with consultancies that are keen to beef up their digital credentials.

I think could be an excellent fit for an organization like that because there's sort of instant credibility there with the, with the legacy of the, the brand and the, the historic client base that it's had.
Okay, thank you.
It's a shame crowd is trying to sell.
Okay, so what kind of valuation are you looking for?
What's the number that you want us to get to.
I think I was preparing myself to talk about background, Andy, rather than.
Well, we've gone through the finance and the clients and now we're on the M and A section.

summary.overview: The M&A Exploratory Meeting for QueryClick focused on the company's background, current operations, and the rationale behind its sale as Chris Liversidge prepares to concentrate on Corvidae, the associated AI attribution platform. Founded in 2008, QueryClick has evolved into a reputable full-service digital marketing agency, generating annual revenues of £1.2-1.4 million and boasting an impressive client roster that includes T-Mobile and Vodafone. The meeting outlined key leadership roles, operational structures, and the company's strategic positioning, emphasizing its potential for growth under new ownership. A target valuation of £9-15 million was proposed, with preferred deal structures and timelines discussed, alongside immediate action items for both the QueryClick team and the advisory group to gather necessary financial and marketing information in preparation for potential buyers. The meeting concluded with a plan to communicate effectively and coordinate efforts to facilitate the M&A process efficiently.
